ATH OR FEMALE DRAGOON.—A widow
who bore herself honorably in the military
service of France, died last week in the Hospice
des Invalides, in Paris, at the age of 87.

Her maiden name was Therese Figueur, and
she served as a dragoon in the 18th and 9th
regiments from 1858 to 1872. She was known
throughout the army by the name of Sans-Gene,
and was so much esteemed by her officers
that when the Committee of Public Safety
ordered the exclusion of all women from the
army an exception was made in her favor.
The history of her campaigns was published
from her own dictation in 1872. She began her
military career at Toulon, when that port was
held by the English in 1803. She was
once under arrest by Commandant Bonapart,
only delay of 15 minutes in executing an
order. 10 years after, when her old Commander
had become First Consul, he sent for
Sans-Gene to St. Cloud and after
rewarding her good service pension of 200
francs, she remained in active service
until she fell into the hands of the
Spanish guerrillas in Spain, and was
taken prisoner of war to England, where
she remained until 1814. In the course of her
many campaigns, she had four horses killed
and was often wounded, the first
at Toulon, when a ball struck her
in the breast. She entered the hospice in
the midst of her pension of 200, till
the Emperor made handsome additions
from his private purse.

Commendable.—We yesterday heard of an incident worthy of notice, and one which might very properly be initiated in these troublous times. The members of a firm engaged in a manufacturing business in this city, few days since went to their landlord and informed him that they intended to vacate his warehouse, assuring him that they were unable on account of the pressure of the crisis to pay the rent they had been paying him formerly and intended procuring a room in a second story at small rent. The landlord replied that as they were young men, just commencing business, he was disposed to assist them, and offered them the use of his warehouse at the same rent for which they could have a second story room in less desirable quarters; he told them that when times got better he would expect them to retain the warehouse, and if they never did improve the rent could be increased upon them.


Proposed Sale of Property.—An ordinance was introduced into the First Branch of the City Council last evening, authorizing the Water Board to sell all land and property other effects acquired by them and not required for the completion of said works, and also to issue notes to the amount of $100,000 for the completion of the works, the same to be paid within two years, from the revenue arising from the sale of the property if the proceeds should be sufficient, and if not that the notes be paid out of the revenue of the Water Works.


A character occurred yesterday, and were it not for the bustle occasioned by the continual passing to and fro of the large military force now on duty in our city, we might say that Baltimore had returned into her former quietude. The streets were somewhat crowded yesterday with gaily-attired ladies and soldiers in full and fatigue uniforms. In fact Baltimore street presented a gala appearance, and with the exception of the soldiers who were to be seen at almost every step, no traces of war's alarms were visible.


A Rumor.—It was currently rumored throughout the city yesterday that a train of cars had been despatched from Philadelphia carrying a large force of workmen and timber with a view to repairing the bridges which have been destroyed upon the line of the road. We have made diligent inquiry, but from such information as we have obtained, we believe the rumor is without any foundation, no such train having been heard of as yet.


Steamer Fired Upon.—It is stated by those on board the steamer George Weems of this city, which arrived here on Wednesday night last, that when passing near Annapolis a shot was fired at her from a steamer lying off the town. The Baltimore steamer paid no attention, the shot falling in her wake and escaped all injury. Several large war steamers loaded with troops are reported off the harbor.


Foundling.—A officer discovered a basket upon the footway corner of Pratt and Howard streets, about eight o'clock Wednesday evening, which was found to contain a male child about ten days old, which had been deposited there by its inhuman mother. A large quantity of clothing was also packed in the basket, and the little outcast was apparently well provided with everything but home. It was taken care of by a lady named Mrs. Meacks.


A Rumor of Settlement.—There was yesterday in circulation a rumor to the effect that the Federal Government had made overtures to Virginia and Maryland, the purport of which was that if the two States named would pledge themselves to protect the Capital at Washington, Mr. Lincoln would order the return of the Northern troops now concentrating at Washington.


Child Burned.—A child of Mr. John Marsh residing at No. 11 Pennsylvania avenue near St. Marys street, was severely burned yesterday afternoon, whilst playing with some matches. A physician was called in, but the child will not be well for some years.


Removal of Headquarters.—Major Trimble, the commander-in-chief of all the volunteer forces under arms, yesterday removed his Headquarters to a room in the second story of the Exchange Reading Room building on second street which has been handsomely fitted up for his accommodation; volunteer militia should be addressed to that office.


Property Sale.—Mr. J. B. Cannon, auctioneer, sold yesterday at the Exchange reading rooms, on second street, a lot of ground situated on West Lexington street, near Stricken, with front of 25 feet, and depth of 80 feet; improved with three-story brick dwelling, and subject to a ground rent of $3.50 per annum; purchased by Christopher West for $100.


Accident.—Mr. Harrison Green, living near Catonsville, on the York road, was injured quite painfully yesterday morning by being run over by his own vehicle, an express wagon, beside which he was walking, when, by his misstep, he was precipitated beneath the wheels which passed over his legs near the knees, injuring him very severely. He was taken to his home by some of the neighbors.


Preparing for an Emergency.—There has been quite an eager demand for flour and in fact all kinds of provisions for the past day or two; the grocery establishments have been overrun with customers. Every resident who is able appears to have provided himself with stock sufficient to last them for some time to come.


Arrival from Montgomery.—Col. Jas. S. Piner, one of Walker's officers in Nicaragua, arrived in this city yesterday from Montgomery, Ala. He reports that the news of the array in our streets reached Montgomery on Friday night, and caused a stirring speech.


Adjustments.—The restrictions on places of amusement having been removed by the Police Commissioners, the several places of resort were crowded last evening, and will no doubt continue to be well patronized.


Steamer for Gov. Hicks.—It was stated that a steamer left here last evening for the purpose of bringing Gov. Hicks to the city as in many directions forwarded here by the messenger from Annapolis.

THE OLD MARYLAND LINE.

In these revolutionary times a brief history of the Maryland Line may not be without interest to the reader. The first battle of the Revolution was fought in North Carolina, on the Albemarle River, and not in New England, as has been always asserted and believed. [Lossings Field Book of the Revolutions, Vol. 2, page 440.] No hotter demonstration was made in that quarter until their attack on Charleston in 1780, when powerful British fleets was driven back with terrible slaughter by the volunteer companies of South Carolina commanded by Colonel Moultrie. It is worthy of remark, that not a single private soldier from New England ever crossed Mason and Dixon's line during the whole war of the Revolution, and in fact never came further south than Long Island except a detachment of Rhode Island troops, sent to occupy Fort Mercer, on the Delaware River, near Philadelphia. Hardily had hostilities commenced in New England before troops were embodied in Maryland and Virginia and marched to the camp at Boston.

The Maryland companies were composed of townsmen. Before the close of July they took up their march for Boston; and they arrived in August. In Cressap's company, numbered one hundred and thirty men, who were armed with tomahawks and rifles, were painted like Indians, and dressed in hunting shirts and moccasins. They exhibited their skill and daring in Frederick, before they set out to the North, the most expert holding the target with their hands for others to shoot at.

After aiding in driving the British from Boston we next end the old Maryland Line at the battle of Long Island. The Northern troops were routed and driven from the field, when the Marylanders covered their retreat and saved them from destruction. Heardly a North Carolina writer, in his Life of Washington, speaking of Stirling, who led the Maryland troops in their terrible charge against the overwhelming force of the British:

"Calling around him portions of Smallwood's glorious regiment of Marylanders, composed almost entirely of young men of rank and wealth, he hurled them with such terrible impetuosity on the British grenadiers, that the latter recoiled with amazement from the shock. Flushed, however, with the previous easy success, and disdaining to yield to a band of undisciplined rebels, they rallied to the attack, and the conflict became close and murderous. But these gallant young men, one and another, pressed so sternly and resolutely into the fray, that they bore down all opposition, and for the first time in open combat rolled back the veterans of England."

Another historian says:

"As they drew out between the two bodies of opposing enemy, it was shouted from the camp, that they were soon to surrender; but with great courage they rushed on their charge upon the opposing force. Terror and sorrow filled every heart, and Washington himself wrung his hands, and exclaimed, Good God, what brave fellows! Five times this little band charged upon the power of Cornwallis; and each time driven back, again gathered their energies for a second assault, until at last upon the sixth, the heavy column of the British yielded under the repeated shocks, and began to give way in confusion.

But at the very moment that victory seemed within their grasp, as great brigades of British, with fresh troops, the brigades of De Treize, came to the aid of Cornwallis in force, they numbered more than ten to one. Now they were overwhelmed by the sheer force; and soon, as they were thrown down by repeated blows, the exhausted men could no longer resist. The Maryland troops in this intense battle were mercilessly attacked. A strong resistance until the last, but they were soon broken, and then the rest of the army was also routed; had they maintained their basis, two brigades of the enemy would have been lost."

in the disaffected States would be considered
tantamount to coercion. This was the state of
things when Mr. Lincoln was inaugurated, a little over two months since. How different
the attitude of men and parties now.

exploded. Nobody now, advocates such an
absurdity. But on the contrary, all unite in
the declaration that the integrity of the Union
must be preserved inviolate at all hazards. All
can see that peaceable secession strikes at the
very foundation of our government and can only
be tolerated at the expense of this great American Republic with all its noble and free institutions, and the destruction of all the glorious hopes that have so long clustered around
this land of the free and home of the brave.

here and there traitors, stigmatized as such by

the battle, or contributing money to carry on
the war, there is no party distinction at the
moment.

have been achieved by the Administration in
the two short months it has been in power, and
who shall say that they will no be mere potent
in putting down this unnatural rebellion and
restoring peace to the country than would have
been half dozen victories over the rebels on
the battle field. The South is now without
prestige or sympathy north of Mason & Dixon
line, and it knows it, and that fact is having

and these effects are daily becoming more and
more apparent.

the impotence of those good Republicans who
are so ready to find fault or complain of halting

Another difficulty the President has had to
contend with, is the number of unreliable men
with which many of the offices both in the Army
and Navy, as well as in the civil service, were

as they claimed, they did not have an equal

then, we have a good beginning made in disposing
of the vexatious controversy which has long been so
fruitlessly joined over the common domain. And
in this fact we have striking proof in evidence of
the inordinate importance attached to mere party
platforms, which, whether good or bad, are general-
ly equally futile, since the practical administration
of the Government is always determined by other
considerations than those which form the basis of
political appeal in the heats of an animated canvass.
As one of the well known sayings of the present At-
torney General, "they are commonly made in times of
high excitement under pressure of circumstances,
and with the view to conciliate present support ra-
ther than to establish a permanent system of princi-
ples and line of policy for the future good govern-
ment of the country. The Conventions which form
them are transient in their nature; their power and
influence are consumed in the using, leaving no con-
tinuing obligation upon their respective parties.
And hence we need not wonder that platforms so
made are hardly ever acted upon in practice."—Nat. Int.

interested, I think it due myself not to pre-

strued.

have used these severe expressions.

men who enlisted in the army, and "being
thought better of it," then invoked my
protection, made the basis of Mr. Russell's
statement, or, as you call it, "monstrous
invention." But it is a fact that since the
25th of April to this present day, with very

In order to justify secession as a constitutional remedy it must be on the principle that the Federal Government is a mere voluntary association of States, to be dissolved at pleasure by one of the contracting parties. If this be so, the Confederacy is a rope of sand, and to be penetrated and dissolved by the first adverse wave of public opinion in any of the States. In this manner our thirty-three States may resolve themselves into as many petty, jarring and hostile Republics, each one retiring from the Union without responsibility whenever any sudden excitement might impel them to such a course. GEORGETOWN, Oct. 31, 1861.


GEORGE C. CORFAX, Esq. My Dear Sir:
I am in receipt of your letter of September 30th, in which you call my attention to certain rumors in the public prints to the effect that I am "endeavoring to bring about a reconciliation among the leaders of the two Democratic wings." You desire me to tighten my friends as to my position, and to say whether or not there is any foundation for any such statement and whether or not you would advise your old Democratic friends to associate themselves politically upon any terms whatever with those who were active and leading supporters of John McConnell at the last election.


I confess that your letter and inquiries surprise me very much. I cannot conceive how any man who pays attention to public affairs, can fail to understand my position in regard to parties, or in regard to the question to which these matters directly refer, that of loyalty to the Government.


Those statements are made by uninformed or idle persons for sensation purposes; or for the meaner purpose of injuring me. Were I not convinced of your friendship for myself, as well as your devotion to the cause of the Union, I would not respond to the interrogations made. But lest my silence on the subject now should mislead any one, I will frankly tell you how I stand. If every man in California were against the Union, and against using the power of the Government to preserve itself, I would be for both; against the people; and I would seek some other place of abode. My opinions do not grow out of the influences of my neighbors, but are the result of my love of country and my estimate of its value.


I have not associated, nor will I not knowingly, associate myself with men who are secessionists, disunionists or traitors; nor will I advise others to do so. Treason is as foul a crime now as it was in the time of Benedict Arnold; and West Point was not worth any more then than Manassas is now. Any opposition to our present nationality is treasonable, pending war, and ought to be punished by banishment from the State, or incarceration in prison. Upon the terms of Union can have political association, and upon none other. I care not whether my associates come from one party or another, so long as they are true upon the one vital point. No party can now be useful except to the extent to which they contribute to the great cause. To the Democratic party as Buchanan made it, I am opposed. To the Democratic party as Douglas would redeem it, I am firmly attached and devoted but my attachment and devotion to it goes no farther than the extent to which it can be made useful to the universal cause of civil liberty. You will perceive that with me the Union is above party. It is a crime now, to raise party above country, or to consider personal interests, pending the greatest danger to all we have, as people, that is worth preserving. That there are partisans base enough to do so we know. Many of them show more talent for getting office, than patriotism or a taste for war but these things will be, no matter how much you and I may regret them.


Attempts to make political parties by specific agreements, and divisions of spoils, will always fail, and are only made by narrow and bad men. Parties must grow out of current necessities and great causes, as well as continue to serve them, or they cannot continue to exist.


To conclude however, I have but one desire, which is, that this Government may be more firmly established in the fear and love of our people, that its prosperity may be continued and that it may be securely transmitted to those who are to succeed us.


I remain, truly, your friend,


JOHN CONFESS.

In sketching brief story of the Revolution

author and gentleman recently drew the
following brilliant and indignant contrast be-

purpose for which it is now used—in which

cued, and has been shown by him to us. We
think it peculiarly appropriate to the present
time. The author, we may well say, has done
more than any other writer to illustrate the
early and heroic annals and social life of his
native State, which he evidently loves with the
earnest piety and reverence of true filial devo-
tion. In proof of that devotion, is the honor-
able fact that he was one of the first mem-
bers of Capt. Randolph's Howitzers, and is
now in active service, ready to shed his blood
to protect the soil of Virginia, as he has been
to give his genius to celebrate her glory.
When such men as Mr. John Esten Cooke, of
quiet life and elegant studies, drop the pen for
the sword and fall into the ranks as common sol-
diers, in the common cause, the tyrants at
Washington may know something of the fire
of honest patriotism, and noble spirit of inde-
pendence which universally inspires the Virgi-
nia people. Let the following eloquent lines
kindle even nobler ardor of devotion than
that which now burns in every bosom:


"Dunmore, the vulgar tyrant of the South,
had fled from the Virginia capital, and the col-
onies were in open resistance against the Crown.
Virginia was on fire, and the county of York
had especial reason to take interest in the
crisis. Dunmore had fled to his ships, and
supplied them with the means of absconding
when he found himself in danger. He
duly did bade brave defiance to the Virgi-
nians whom he had deceived before and di-
rected his subordinates to ravage the sur-
rounding coasts of the Bay.


That was in olden time; and now, to-day, Virginia
is again terrorised. She threw the gauntlet
down to England for the liberties of all the
States. She gave her Jefferson to pen the
august declaration, setting forth the rights of
man, and making common cause with all.
Her Henry set the mighty axe in motion;
and her Washington led the great host of
brethren, fighting for their freedom—led them
through storm and fire, through snow and
blood from the heights of Boston to the re-
doubts of Yorktown, where the curtain was
to fall upon the great drama of 'America De-
fended.'


That was the record of the past; but now
to-day,


To dey, within morning's ride of the
sacred soil of Yorktown, where the patriots of
the North and the South, thrilled with com-
mon triumph and common glory—to-day,
the foaming guns of Fortress Monroe—placed
there to sweep the sea horizon outposts, and
protect Virginia—are levelled inward, to in-
timidate the sons and grandsons of the men
who poured their heart's blood out for the free-
dom of the sovereign States.


Virginia is menaced from the soil she ceded
to drive back foreign foe—and the hand
that turned those cannon of the fortress in-
ward—the hand which we are told is now
raised against the South—against Virginia.


But another hand. The hand of him who
has brought against that great and august
name. Nothing so poor-proof as strong as
holy writ—proof sir, and accepted with hot tears—shall prompt a simple word of
scorn for the hero of a hundred fights.


If it be that age has dimmed the vision of
the soldier—sophistry has clouded the im-
perial brain—the thing we look on, is a mighty
people gone to ruin—an awful and pathetic
spectacle of fallen grandeur.


Let us pause before that word of scorn is
uttered—let us cling to our disbelief as mar-
tyrs cling to their faith: and then, if the issue
be the woeful issue which his foes predict, let
us turn, with averted faces, from the tomb
where lies enmeshed too much of greatness and
of glory.


Alas the hissing words of scorn must now
be uttered, and resounded through all the com-
mon ages; the tomb of infamy must now be
opened, and the name and fame of Winfield
Scott be buried there forever! The honored
and favored child has turned too on the land
and liberties of his fathers—the unnatural
traitor brandishes aloft his sordid sword above
the venerable head of his mother, and threatens "to bathe it in the blood of her bosom!" as

mother; the ranking memory of fancied
slight, ten years ago; the inspiration of hate
that unfolds itself in organized fleets and
armies to invade her soil and desolate her shores.


Can this be so! Let us rather trust that
age has dimmed the vision; that sophistry
has clouded the brain of the dotard Chief, and
let us, his friends, indulge the painful hope
that Death, in kindness, will soon come to his
rescue, and relieve him from the melancholy
infamy, which will cure."

BIRMINGHAM, Dec. 2.—The Times article,
of the 30th of November, shows that the fall of two
per cent in consols and four per cent in shares
while the question of actual war is altogether unde-
cided, is not justified by the nature of things. Be-
tween January and March, 1854, when war was de-
clared against Russia consols went from 99½ to 98,
and within six months they had recovered to 91¼.
Yet the rate of discount at the time of the outbreak
was nearly twice as high as at present, and the stock
of bullion at the bank was considerably lower.
Throughout the entire struggle the value of money
was unaltered beyond the extent of one per cent.
The railway traffic remained good, and the business
of the country went on satisfactorily.

The position of the Federal States of America is
almost identical in every commercial point with that
which was occupied toward us by Russia. Russia
had hostile tariffs, while locked to her for a
large portion of our general supply of bread.
But there is this peculiarly in our present case, that
the commencement would be by breaking up the
blockade of the Southern ports at once, set free our
industry from the anxiety of a cotton famine, and
give prosperity to Lancashire through the winter.
At the same time we shall open our trade to eight
who desire nothing better than to be our customers. With respect
to necessary consideration also the contrast between
the two periods is all in our favor. In 1851 we were
totally unprepared for war, and had to procure
everything, but now by the large but unprecedented
outlay of the past three years, we have attained a
degree of efficient power such as was never before
known.

The mischief was, Arthur was dependent upon his mother; she should, for our peace, have been dependent upon him.

From that moment her reign was absolute. To satisfy her son, who really had little pride at the bottom of his incidence, she made him her man of business, giving him handsome allowance for collecting rents, writing mortgages, and cashing checks.

The hardest thing to understand was, why she permitted him to marry me, who had not a penny of fortune, nothing in fact, but finished education, respectable name, a tolerably pretty face, and—I am not troubled with modesty—as much sense as any woman of my size. I don't think I have quite solved the problem yet. Perhaps she hoped to have more influence over a dependent daughter-in-law; possibly because Arthur was sometimes—not often—addicted to having his own sweet will. We were seldom brought in contact, and I knew little about her. She did not object, and rooms in an uptown boarding house were engaged for Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Burney.

Now commenced my novitiate to my new relative. She cooed about me like a wooing dove.

Our privacy (and every couple knows how delightful that is during the first few weeks of matrimony) she invaded at all hours, ostensibly with the most motherly motives, but really to keep herself informed of our comings and goings. My wardrobe was scrutinized, and its value quickly determined by her keen, calculating eyes. My books were examined and criticised; my correspondence inquired into. In two weeks, Mrs. Burney, senior, knew more about me than I intended she should in two years; but her manner was so unobjectionable, her questioning and cross-questioning so artful, that at that early date she was more than a match for me.

My husband's mother should have been counselor-at-law. Pitt in his palmiest days never asked more subtle questions, or gave more polite answers. She never assumed a position that was untenable, nor committed the blunder of losing her temper. The only discrepancy was, she gave her verdicts before she heard the evidence.

All this was accomplished by the cool, calm, pleasant, polite lady, with not the least appearance of interference or surveillance. She was well-bred to the last degree. She seldom made direct charges, or faulted me openly; covert hints gracefully thrown out, or insinuations covered with the veil of motherly interest made her motive scarcely perceptible, but served her purpose as well. I had my suspicions, my misgivings; but this espionage was conducted so skillfully, that I had been several months a bride before I realized the humiliation of my position. I had been a bond-slave; no fetters of iron could have held me closer than my husband's mother held me. I and Arthur were human chattels, nothing more—subsisting on her substance, obeying her will. She had prestige of power about her, such magnetism in her tone and manner, that I submitted in very awe, hardly daring to ask myself why I did so.

One day after a series of inquiries and insidious comments respecting some of my friends, whom my fastidious mother-in-law thought were not eligible acquaintances for her son's wife, I startled her and myself by suddenly declaring that I felt quite competent to make out my visiting list, and desired to be allowed to do so. It was slightly disrespectful, and was also slightly true. Mrs. Burney looked me over with her hard gray eyes, as if she contemplated transfixing me with her glances. Somehow, those same glances had suddenly lost the power. The little imp, Rebellion, had fairly taken possession of me—and with his saucy eye, I shot back such defiance that the lady made a skillful retreat from my presence.

I went to Arthur; I might as well have appealed to a lazy opium-eater. He was sleeping, and I hoped I wouldn't disturb him. He was certain his mother knew best about social caste. "Miss Stewart, or Miss Brown, did not belong to her set"; it was proper that I should cut the ties at once, and adopt her advice, like a reasonable woman.

"Do not be so intensely heartless and selfish, Arthur," I indignantly exclaimed.

"I am not selfish; I am simply sensible. When you have lived longer, Ellen, you will know more."

"Dear me! What Methuselah of age, and Solomon of wisdom, I have in my husband! Are you four or five months my senior?"

"Don't be sarcastic, Ellen. My mother said no real lady permits herself to be sarcastic."

The Young Zouaves, Captain Rodier, numbering twenty-six, and the Junior Potomac Rifles,

both from Georgetown, also paraded in the
morning. The Zouaves were equipped with
musketoons, and the Junior Rifles with little
carbines. They made fine appearance, maneuvered exceedingly well, and elected much
praise from those who witnessed their movements.

The battalion of marines were drilled in the
morning in the barrack yard. They numbered
over two hundred men on parade, and made
very fine appearance.

By consent of Commissioner Blake, the ladies
caused a beautiful silk flag, bearing the words
"Peace! Peace! Peace!" to be placed in
the right hand of the statue, in such a position
that the drapery of our glorious national ensign
fell in loving and graceful folds by the right
hand of the Father of his Country.

now in the city, which was countermanded on

The story which has been going the rounds of the Northern press in regard to a disagreement between General Lee and the President in regard to the plan of the campaign is, I am informed, true. The enemy no doubt discovered the horses of the generals, and thought it a good opportunity to display their marksmanship, and credit is due to them for the accuracy of their aim.

THE CRISIS OF THE BATTLE.

They pressed our left flank for several hours with terrible effect, but our men hinched not until their numbers had been diminished by the well aimed and steady volleys, that they were compelled to give way for new regiments. The seventh and eighth Georgia regiments commanded by the gallant and lamented Barlow, are said to have suffered heavily during the early part of the battle. Kempers, Shields, and Pendleton's batteries were in this part of the field, and did fearful execution.

I am inclined to believe there was some mistake during the day, in the delivery or execution of an order of Gen. Beauregard's respecting an attack on the enemy's rear, which was not effected.

Between two and three o'clock large numbers of men were leaving the field, some of them wounded, others exhausted by the long struggle, who gave us gloomy reports; but as the fire on both sides continued steadily, we felt sure that our brave Southerners had not been conquered by the overwhelming hordes of the North. It is, however, due to truth to say that the result at this hour hung trembling in the balance. We had lost numbers of our most distinguished officers. Generals Barlow and Lee had been stricken down; Lieut. Colonel Johnson, of the Hampton Legion, had been killed; Col. Hampton had been wounded, but there was at hand the fearless General whose reputation as a commander was staked on this battle; and with that chivalry which is his nature, General Beauregard promptly offered to lead the Hampton Legion into the action, which he executed in a style unsurpassed and unsurpassed.

Your correspondent heard Gen. Johnston exclaim to Gen. Cooke, just at the critical moment, "Oh for four regiments!" His wish was answered, for in the distance our reinforcements appeared.

The tide of the battle was turned in our favor by the arrival of Gen. Kirby Smith, from Winchester, with four thousand men of Gen. Johnston's division. General Smith heard, while on the Manassas Railroad cars, the roar of battle. He stopped the train and hurried his troops across the fields to the point just where he was most needed. They were at first supposed to be the enemy, their arrival at that point of the field being entirely unexpected.

day morning, Oct 28th, 1861, upon the

death of John French.

Babylon was a royal city, and, as such

attracted the attention of the world.

Perhaps no city ever existed possessing

more wealth, refinement of taste, or proficiency in the arts and sciences. Certainly none ever existed more strongly fortified, or better supplied with sustenance and hence better able to withstand open assault or protracted siege, than she. Around about her on either side, were walls of solid masonry, so high that they might not be scaled, so strong that no known enginery of war could make any breach therein. Within her, were most extensive storehouses, filled to overflowing with all needed supplies, to sustain her many thousands of inhabitants for a century, and through the midst of her ran the waters of mighty river. To human view, her supplies were inexhaustible.

Who would suppose a city thus fortified, thus supplied, could be in danger from any foe, be it never so strong or vigilant: Certainly not her own citizens—surely not her king. Resting in simplest security, the King of this mighty city gave a banquet, and the city was devoted to the hilarity, the pleasures, and, it may be, the dissipation of the hour, in the midst of which besieging foe turned the waters of the river from their wonted course, and marched through the channel of the stream, under the walls, into the heart of the city, and, in an hour, struck the fatal blow which slaughtered her citizens, laid her king under the yoke, razed to the ground her temples and her palaces, her statues and her walls, leaving the site whereon she stood desolated, waste even unto the present day.

And the record of this sudden, complete and terrible destruction is found in the words of Revelation—“Her sun set while it was yet noon.” No more expressive or significant language could well be chosen, to express the magnitude or the suddenness of such desolation. “Her sun set while it was yet noon.”

Let us comprehend the thought. Let us appreciate the full force of the idea.—Suppose that tomorrow, at high twelve, while all of you were engaged in your ordinary avocations, suddenly, without premonition or alarm, the mighty laws upon the constant and regular operation of which Universe depends, should all at once cease their operation, or take on perverse action, and the darkness of midnight should fall upon you by the sun setting “while it was yet noon.” As this would be in the natural world to you, so would it be with a city, her very existence put out at its meridian, in a single hour, and the night of civil death brooding over her. “Her sun set while it was yet noon!”

Having obtained full possession of the idea, let us, in the light of it, behold the man who, having lived out but half his allotted years—the “three score years and ten”—when, by reason of strength, they number “four score,” by means of industry and frugality, having amassed a competence by years of sobriety, honesty and high moral conviction, having made fair and valuable character, a spotless reputation; his generosity having made him the friend and almoner of the humble and the poor; his learning making him the safe counselor of the rich and the strong; his loyalty making him a pillar in the state; is suddenly arrested in the midst of all these, by mortal illness and death, and removed from all the busy scenes of life, the cold earth closing in upon the loved form, and hiding him from human gaze. Of such an one what more fitting record can be made, than that his “sun set while it was yet noon!”

Alas! my friends, you and I, this entire community, all at once have had thrust upon us, in the most emphatic manner, an illustration of the great propriety and force of the train of thought above traced, in the death of our neighbor, our friend and brother, JOHN FRENCH, Esq., who was man in the noon of life, in the full practice of an honorable profession, enjoying the love and confidence of all who knew him; kind and faithful husband, a liberal neighbor, loyal citizen; and yet he died, died suddenly, has passed away. How better can we express the idea, the fact of such an one's death, under such circumstances, than by exclaiming, “His sun set while it is yet noon!”

So due out in much was studied, because he possessed and exemplified so many of the virtues, and so few of the infirmities of human nature, because of his value to community and the state, and because of your love for the pure, the generous and the noble in man, is it that you have met here tonight, as one great family, to testify your respect for our friend, and, in fitting manner, manifest your sorrow for the loss of one of your most valued members.

Most manifestly, an individual must possess many virtues, must have lived a blameless life, manifesting many of the beatitudes and none of the perversities of human nature, who, after years of active public, official, professional life, is able, in his death, to command the respect of an entire community, and the commingling of its tears over the grave wherein he slumbers. And what a reward to virtue, to generosity, to learning, to loyalty! What an inducement to the young, in starting out on the journey of life, to choose only the highway of virtue and goodness, and to persistently follow it, turning neither to the right nor the left, nor yet leering on the way, but marching.
